name: Shelter
label: Revelation
lede: Youth of Today's singer shaved his head, took vows, and brought a busload of monks on tour with a hardcore band, and for a few years in the '90s the pit was full of tulasi beads.

eras.title: The last Youth of Today record gets a new name
eras.text: Youth of Today was winding down and Ray Cappo had come back from India a Krishna devotee. He meant to make one final record about what he now believed, a farewell to punk's material world. Revelation Records heard it and decided it was a new band.

years.cap: The debut, released on Revelation the same year as Youth of Today's last album
years.h: Perfection of Desire: a solo farewell turns into a band
years.p: Cappo's goodbye record comes out on Revelation under the name Shelter, the shelter a devotee takes in a guru and, finally, in Krishna. The credits read like a roll call at the temple: first names only.
years.xp:
The idea was vegetarianism and straight edge followed to their end point: a spiritual life. Cappo wrote the songs as a statement of faith, and Revelation made the call to put them out as a new band rather than a Cappo solo record.

[[Sammy Siegler|869c662b-574c-46ac-acf6-3dc6f025fd5a]], who had joined Youth of Today at 15, says he drummed two songs on that first release.

years.h: Cappo starts a label to spread the word
years.p: Equal Vision Records opens in Albany, New York, with one job: getting Shelter and other Krishna releases into the world.

eras.title: Monks in the van
eras.text: Shelter became a traveling temple. The lineup changed constantly, some players were celibate devotees and some were hardcore kids who liked the music, and the shows mixed chanting, vegetarian food and a pit. Hardcore gave it a name, sometimes as a sneer: Krishnacore.

years.p: The second record keeps the message front and center. Cappo will remake its title track on his 2006 solo album fifteen years later.
He holds it until 1993, and he'll be back in the lineup twenty-five years later.

years.h: Quest for Certainty: two bands on one record
years.p: The Revelation credits split it down the middle. Tracks 1 to 4: [[Vic DiCara|a6698e1f-db17-4e93-9c4f-56678238e91f]], Interrante and Eric Dailey. Tracks 5 and 6: [[Porcell|dff848b4-bb79-445a-81e1-3db65b7ddd3e]], Graham Land, a bassist credited as Yashomatinandana, and a drummer listed only as Sam.

years.h: Cappo sells Equal Vision to the man running it
years.p: Label manager Steve Reddy buys it. The Krishna-only mission widens, and within a few years the label is putting out [[Converge|fa31e7d4-a03a-4110-98fc-f8826e95ec25]], Bane and [[Saves the Day|593f8594-83ad-4df4-a9b8-e4d225f55440]].

years.cap: Devotees in a school bus, the Maharaja in a Winnebago, the non-devotees in a van
q: Dudes in Krishna robes playing hardcore. It was punk, dangerous, and badass.
years.h: The caravan tour: a school bus, a Winnebago and the Conch
years.p: Sammy Siegler, 17, books a tour with [[Inside Out|0049c4d7-6459-4b54-a865-fd19969f427f]] and [[Quicksand|3c9f8bef-a658-4204-9ee8-7e95d2535b32]] off a phone list. Devotees ride in a school bus, the Maharaja in a Winnebago, and [[Zack de la Rocha|aa659468-db56-41c9-b6fe-61f4bb2ef1a6]] and the other non-devotees in a van.
years.xp:
Siegler remembers a fluorescent orange hat called the Conch: whoever held it got to talk. It was the only way to keep order among that many people on one tour.

Inside Out's [[Vic DiCara|a6698e1f-db17-4e93-9c4f-56678238e91f]] would cross over too, playing guitar in Shelter and later forming [[108|7f0c252a-bd45-4fe0-b306-478eeb07b97b]].

years.p: The title says it plainly. Shelter also puts out devotional side releases this year, Shelter Bhajan and Standard Temple Songs.
Cappo's [[Youth of Today|9ca27db4-f127-4aeb-ae87-29e21f558c13]] partner becomes the band's long-serving guitarist and, soon, its co-producer. He stays through 2000.

eras.title: A metal label signs the robes
eras.text: The mid-'90s put Shelter among the biggest hardcore bands going, next to Snapcase, Strife, Earth Crisis and Sick of It All. Roadrunner, home of Type O Negative, signed them, and the band landed on festival stages with Slayer, Venom and the reformed Sex Pistols. It was as close to crossover as Krishnacore ever got.

years.p: Eleven songs in about thirty minutes, produced by Tom Soares and Porcell. The booklet carries a manifesto by Cappo called Supersoul, which becomes the name of his imprint.
years.xp:
[[Dave DiCenso|fba8fbad-b75b-409a-8e91-4ef7cbb17605]] plays drums on the record. Sammy Siegler helped write the material but isn't on it. The songs pair Krishna philosophy with a running critique of Western life, in titles like Civilized Man and Surrender to Your T.V.

Critics split along the obvious line. Trouser Press called Cappo a principled spokesman for transcendental thought set to a tough 4/4 beat. Germany's Ox-Fanzine, looking back, heard a tame rock album from another time.

years.h: On tour with Type O Negative
years.p: Labelmates on Roadrunner, the two bands share a bill that Siegler says kind of worked. On the road, a devotee hosts them for dinner at a saffron-painted mansion.
The Brazilian edition of Mantra adds two bonus tracks, one of them a cover of the Beatles' We Can Work It Out. The band plays Brazil for the first time.
The second and last Roadrunner album. The tours now run across North America, Europe and South America.

eras.title: Twenty summers, then quiet
eras.text: By the turn of the century the Krishna wave in hardcore had crested, and Shelter pulled back from full-time preaching. Two more albums on two more labels, one last run of shows, and then a hiatus nobody called a breakup.

years.p: A new label for a new decade. It's also the year Porcell's first run in the band ends.
Released on Cappo's own imprint. The band tours Europe and the eastern U.S., then goes on extended hiatus.

eras.title: The door never quite closed
eras.text: Shelter came back in pieces: a European tour, a Cappo record under the band's name, a pair of one-off shows on two continents. Cappo had moved to California by then; he'd later settle in upstate New York as a yoga teacher.

years.p: A reunion tour takes Shelter overseas, where the audience never really went away.
Essentially a Cappo solo album: ten new songs plus a remake of In Defense of Reality. A European tour follows.
The first of two reunion shows ten days apart, on either side of the Atlantic.
The second one, back home.

eras.title: Punk to monk to the Dome
eras.text: The classic players regrouped, Cappo wrote it all down, and Mantra came back on vinyl at thirty. In 2026 it gets billed as the other half of a Youth of Today night.

years.p: Cappo, [[Porcell|dff848b4-bb79-445a-81e1-3db65b7ddd3e]], [[Sammy Siegler|869c662b-574c-46ac-acf6-3dc6f025fd5a]] and Chris Interrante play a U.S. tour and a European festival. Siegler is back behind the kit twenty-eight years after he drummed on the first record.
Ray Raghunath Cappo's memoir comes out on Mandala Publishing, with a foreword by [[Moby|8970d868-0723-483b-a75b-51088913d3d4]].
An anniversary vinyl edition puts the Roadrunner album back in record stores.

years.h: Two nights at the Dome, London
years.p: Cappo is billed to front both [[Youth of Today|9ca27db4-f127-4aeb-ae87-29e21f558c13]] and Shelter, the band he started when the first one ended.
